surprises.description: Investors were looking for the 2026 copper-volume plan to be reaffirmed, but FCX cut copper sales guidance by about 2% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2027, citing lower U.S. and Chile production. The cuts are a negative deviation from the expected reaffirmation, even though 2027 production is still forecast to grow substantially.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company cut its 2026 copper sales guidance by about 2% and 2027 guidance by about 2.5% due to lower U.S. and Chile production.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 volume reaffirmation (3.1B lbs Cu / 650k oz Au). The buy-side expects a reaffirm.”

surprises.description: The expected Grasberg ramp to 80% capacity by mid-2027 was reiterated, but near-full capacity is now targeted for year-end 2028 rather than the preview’s expectation of full capacity by year-end 2027. That pushes the completion of the recovery about a year later than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Grasberg reached 67% of mine capacity in Q3 2026, with management targeting 80% by mid-2027 and near-full capacity by year-end 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “80% of capacity by mid-2027, full capacity by year-end 2027.”

surprises.description: The preview expected 2027 guidance to be deferred, but FCX gave a capital-spending figure and raised 2027 capex by about $400 million to $5.2 billion. The Bagdad expansion decision is expected in Q4, but its roughly $4.5 billion cost is not included in that 2027 capex figure, leaving a large project commitment outside the stated budget.
surprises.fact_evidence: “2027 capital expenditure guidance was raised about $400 million to $5.2 billion”; “A Bagdad expansion investment decision is expected in Q4 2026 at a roughly $4.5 billion cost”; “no amount included in 2027 capex guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “2027 formally deferred to the December/January guidance release”; the preview also flagged “any first-pass 2027 capex figure.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on the risk that costs above the Q3 level could undermine the $1.90/lb full-year target. FCX disclosed an approximately $500 million energy-cost increase, including more than doubled diesel prices, but maintained that unit-cost guidance because molybdenum credits offset the pressure. The cost headwind was substantial, while the maintained guidance was better than the risk scenario implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rising energy costs, led by more than a doubling of diesel prices, added approximately $500 million to costs in 2026 versus 2025, yet 2026 net unit cash cost guidance was maintained at $1.90 per pound thanks to by-product (molybdenum) offsets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If the actual print shows cost pressure beyond the gold deferral — labor, diesel, mining rates, Grasberg fixed-cost absorption — the ‘transitory’ framing breaks and the FY2026 $1.90/lb target ... goes with it.”

surprises.description: The preview noted leach progress toward a 300-million-pound annual target, but the call described a next-generation additive with lab recoveries more than four times those of the initial additive and potential to scale production toward 800 million pounds by 2030. This is a more ambitious longer-term opportunity, although it remains unproven in field testing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A next-generation proprietary leaching additive showed lab recoveries more than 4x the initial additive and will be field-tested in 2027, with potential to scale leach production toward 800 million pounds by 2030.”
